opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that AI for math has been living in a few separate worlds that rarely talk to each other.

On one side, you have the formal methods community: people who have spent years building proof assistants like Lean, and libraries like Mathlib, painstakingly encoding mathematics so a computer can verify every step. That world gives you something incredibly valuable, which is ground truth. If the proof checks, it's correct. There's no hallucination.

On another side, you have the large language model world, which has gotten remarkably good at informal reasoning. These models can sketch an argument, suggest an approach, recall a relevant lemma. But they can also be confidently wrong, and in mathematics, being 95% right is often the same as being wrong.

Then there's a third thread: classical search, program synthesis, reinforcement learning, the kind of thinking that produced systems which explore huge spaces and learn from feedback.

In academia, each of these tends to live in a different department, a different conference, a different culture. A grad student in formal verification and a grad student training language models might never collaborate, not because they don't want to, but because the incentives, compute budgets, and timelines just don't line up.

What I saw was that the real breakthrough probably sits at the intersection. You want models that can think informally and creatively, then translate that thinking into formal language, get verified, and learn from what passes and what fails. That loop, generation, formalization, verification, and learning, needs all of these pieces working together.

And building that loop well is expensive. It takes serious compute, it takes engineers who can build infrastructure at scale, and it takes the patience to work on something for years rather than one paper cycle. A well-funded company can hire the Lean expert, the RL researcher, and the mathematician, put them in the same room, and give them a shared goal. That's very hard to do anywhere else.

There's also a timing element. The models had just become strong enough, and the formal libraries had just become rich enough, that combining them stopped being a thought experiment and became an engineering problem. When something shifts from "is this possible?" to "how do we build it?", that's usually when a focused company can move faster than the existing structures.

So for me it wasn't just about the money. Funding was the means to assemble a team with deliberately different backgrounds and point them all at one very hard, very verifiable target. Mathematics is unusual because you know when you're right. That makes it, I think, one of the best places to build AI that actually reasons.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that when I was doing math research, I kept running into a strange situation. There were basically three different communities all trying to get computers to do mathematics, and they almost never talked to each other.

You had the formal methods people, the Lean and Coq and Isabelle community, who cared deeply about rigor. Every proof is machine-checked, there's no hand-waving, but it's incredibly labor-intensive and most working mathematicians found it too painful to adopt. Then you had the machine learning people, who were training large language models on mathematical text and getting these impressive but unreliable results. The model would write something that looked like a beautiful proof and then there'd be a subtle error in step four. And then you had the actual mathematicians, who mostly thought both groups were a bit beside the point, because the thing they cared about, which is taste, intuition, knowing which problems matter, wasn't being addressed by either side.

Each of those groups had something the others were missing. The formal people had verification. The ML people had scale and the ability to generate candidates. The mathematicians had the judgment about what's worth proving. And it seemed obvious to me that the real breakthrough would come from putting them in the same room, literally the same building, with the same infrastructure.

But the reason that hadn't happened is that academia is structured against it. A math department doesn't hire a systems engineer. A CS department doesn't reward someone for spending two years formalizing a textbook. Grant cycles are short, and the compute you need to train these models is simply not available to a university lab at the scale that matters. So the pieces existed, but nobody had the resources and the institutional freedom to assemble them.

That's the gap an industrial lab can fill. You can hire across disciplines without worrying about departmental boundaries. You can afford the compute. You can run on a five or ten year horizon instead of a three-year grant. And frankly, you can pay people enough that a brilliant mathematician doesn't have to choose between their research and a reasonable life.

What tipped me from thinking about it to actually doing it was watching how fast the language models were improving. Two years earlier I would have said the ML side was too immature for this to work. But once the models could generate plausible proof sketches and the formal tools could check them, you suddenly had a feedback loop. The model proposes, the verifier rejects or accepts, the mathematician steers. That loop only works if all three are tightly integrated, and nobody was building that. So we decided to.

astra-6.text:
I saw an opportunity to bring together approaches that are often pursued separately: language models, formal verification, and the tools mathematicians use to explore ideas. They have complementary strengths. A model can suggest a promising direction, while a formal system can check whether the reasoning actually holds up.

But making those pieces work together takes sustained investment—in researchers, compute, and infrastructure. A well-funded industrial company can give people with different backgrounds the resources and time to work on a shared problem. To me, the opportunity was to build that feedback loop: systems that can explore mathematical ideas creatively and also check their work rigorously.

sol-6.1.text:
I saw an opportunity because AI for mathematics sits at the intersection of several approaches that can really help one another. You have language models that can suggest ideas and proof strategies, formal systems that can check whether a proof is correct, and search methods that can explore possibilities. The interesting question is how to make those pieces work together.

That takes sustained investment. You need mathematicians and machine learning researchers working closely with engineers, and you need infrastructure that lets them experiment and learn from failures. A well-funded company can support that kind of shared effort over time.

For me, the opportunity was to build a place where the mathematical problem drives the choice of methods. You can draw on different research traditions and bring them together around the goal of making progress on mathematics.
